items.summary: Recent achievements in AI-assisted mathematics require intensive interaction of agents with proof assistants to generate machine-checked proof certificates. Agents interact with proof assistants such as Rocq or Lean through an interface that controls what the agent receives from the prover and the cost of these interactions. Today, these interfaces are adapted from tools designed for humans and not optimized for agents. We propose an evolutionary method where a frontier model incrementally proposes new features and only keeps the ones that improve the overall performance of smaller models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by growing, on a curated set of mathematical problems, ROCQ-MCP-EVOLVE, a new MCP server for the Rocq prover. On the held-out test split of miniF2F-Rocq, an agent equipped with ROCQ-MCP-EVOLVE outperforms both the baseline that only exposes the Rocq compiler and an established MCP server, across four models from two families, in success rate, cost per solve, and time per solve. Although evolved for Rocq, the resulting server transfers to Lean, improving cost and time per solve on a subset of PutnamBench. We release ROCQ-MCP-EVOLVE and its port to Lean.
items.title: Growing an Agent/Prover Interface: Evolutionary Tool Design for Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving in Rocq and Lean

items.summary: Solutions to geophysical inverse problems are generally non-unique, and greatly benefit from additional geological prior information. Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are commonly used to parametrise such information, typically restricting solutions to a lower-dimensional latent space. The final inversion result is obtained by mapping the latent space parameters to the original higher-dimensional model space using the GNNs. However, solutions then remain confined to a low-dimensional geological generative manifold; if the true Earth model lies outside of this manifold, standard latent space inversion fails. We propose a Bayesian model space inversion method that uses the generative manifold as a guide to find the solutions that lie outside this manifold. We validate our approach in non-linear travel-time tomography experiments on both simple and more geological structures. By comparing our method with model space inversion using uniform prior probabilities and standard latent-space inversion, we demonstrate that the less informative uniform prior fails to constrain the solution, while the latent space approach fails when the true Earth model lies outside of the generative manifold. Conversely, our new model-space inversion method successfully recovers complex off-manifold geological features while maintaining low solution uncertainty.
items.title: Escaping Geological Generative Prior Distributions in Bayesian Travel Time Tomography

items.summary: Physics-informed machine learning has gained significant attention in recent years. In regimes of limited data, parametrized Gaussian processes have become popular. Existing approaches, however, often face limitations, such as requiring parametrizable (also called controllable) systems or a large number of output tasks. In this work, we introduce a systematic procedure we call "ghost tasking", using auxiliary tasks to circumvent these limitations. We prove that such ghost tasks can render any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling algorithmic construction of parametrized Gaussian Processes while keeping the number of required tasks (i.e. output dimensions) and latent functions low. We find that ghost tasking performs especially well in an inverse problem setting, even with very few available data. We show the usage and power of ghost tasking in three experiments, providing systematic comparisons to the only other currently available method applicable to all experiments. We provide necessary syntax and explications for two computer algebra programs that compute parametrizations for systems with polynomial or rational coefficients. Our theoretical results extend to systems with meromorphic functions.
items.title: Ghost tasking for parametrized Gaussian Processes solving linear differential equations

items.summary: We study the relation between equal-weight circle quadrature, Gauss--Chebyshev quadrature, and planar Minkowski reconstruction. The regular $N$-point grid is an $\mathbb S^1$-design of strength $N-1$; a half-step rotation of the $2M$-point grid projects to the classical $M$-point Gauss--Chebyshev rule. A common family of quadrature-error functionals gives exact identities for integration error, mixed-area error, and support-function error. For $N\ge3$, the centered Minkowski polygon $P_N$ with perimeter $2π$ has the exact Hausdorff distance from the unit disk $B^2$ \[ d_H(P_N,B^2)=1-\fracπ{N}\cot\fracπ{N} =\frac{π^2}{3N^2}+O(N^{-4}). \] With Steiner centering, we obtain $d_H(K_μ,K_ν)\leπW_1(μ,ν)$ for balanced, nondegenerate probability measures, where $W_1$ uses geodesic distance. Its exponent is sharp even for smooth positive densities near the uniform measure. The identity $W_1(ν_N,σ)=π/(2N)$ yields a general $O(N^{-1})$ bound for the regular grid. The sharper $O(N^{-2})$ rate follows from the sparse discrepancy spectrum and the inverse multiplier $(1-k^2)^{-1}$. Finally, a perturbation estimate gives sufficient conditions for preserving the quadratic rate and its leading constant.
items.title: Gauss--Chebyshev Quadrature, $\mathbb S^1$-Designs, and the Planar Minkowski Inverse Problem: A One-Dimensional Model for Design-Induced Convex Geometry

items.summary: We give a written counterexample to the arbitrary-positive-mass statement of Heilman 2019 Conjecture 1.16. For every 0<p<1/4, the mass vector (p,(1-p)/3,(1-p)/3,(1-p)/3) has a strict non-regular improvement. The equal-mass tetrahedral problem is untouched. The record contains the frozen PDF, source package, exact Q(sqrt(2)) diagnostics, partial Lean algebra, and a targeted prior-work comparison. No external peer review or worldwide priority claim is made.
items.title: A facet-exchange counterexample to the fixed-mass regular-simplex conjecture

items.summary: LLM agents can spend millions of tokens during vulnerability discovery without producing a working proof of concept (PoC). What consumes that budget, and why does it fail to produce results? We diagnose these costs and failures through a multi-axis open-coding study of 200 CyberGym traces, spanning four agents (i.e., Codex, OpenCode, Cybench, and EnIGMA) under an unaided baseline and four existing efficiency methods. The study reveals three key findings. First, different agents vary substantially in success and cost, and higher spending does not consistently yield better outcomes. Second, code localization and understanding, together with vulnerability reasoning and trigger design, account for 60.4% of tokens and represent the two leading bottlenecks in failed runs. Third, only 24.4% of matched comparisons preserve success at lower total cost; unsuitable signals and auxiliary overhead limit the benefits of existing methods. Motivated by these findings, we present AVRI, an Agent-centric Vulnerability Reasoning Interface built around a persistent Bidirectional Evidence Trace (BET). BET connects how the harness consumes input with the conditions required to make a selected operation unsafe, retaining source-supported correspondences alongside the agent's hypotheses and open questions. Reading, analysis, and persistence commands help agents build and reuse this evidence rather than repeatedly retrieve and reconstruct it. On 20 evaluation tasks, AVRI reduces total cost by 18.0% for Codex and 23.7% for OpenCode while preserving success rates and improving or maintaining recall.
items.title: Where Do the Tokens Go? Understanding and Reducing Costs in LLM Agents for Vulnerability Discovery

items.summary: Anatomical continuity provides complementary information for medical image restoration, but its use requires accounting for local anatomy and variations in slice sampling. We introduce ContiLNN, which augments two-dimensional restoration backbones with bidirectional closed-form continuous-time (Bi-CfC) modules for cross-slice modeling while retaining in-plane feature extraction. Slice-index intervals modulate gates determined by local features and hidden states, enabling propagation to respond to sampling variations without numerical ODE integration. Reference-guided consistency aligns first- and second-order cross-slice intensity differences to preserve anatomical variation, while distillation from a frozen backbone helps retain in-plane fidelity. Across five training seeds, ContiLNN improves mean PSNR over Restore-RWKV by 0.1907, 1.0176, and 1.2482 dB for CT denoising, MRI super-resolution, and reduced-count PET restoration, respectively, with lower RMSE in all three tasks. CT results are descriptive for one held-out patient. PET ablations support ordered propagation beyond additional pointwise capacity. Under contiguous training, Bi-CfC achieves higher fidelity than a Bi-GRU with similar parameter counts and arithmetic costs across all tested sampling conditions. Matched seven-slice profiling shows 52.8% lower latency and 57.0% lower peak GPU memory use than Bi-GRU. Mixed-gap training improves sparse and irregular-context performance for both operators, without a uniform ranking across metrics and contexts. Experiments with fewer training patients and a second backbone further support data efficiency and backbone compatibility.
items.title: ContiLNN: Mitigating Slice Sampling Discontinuity with Liquid Neural Networks for Medical Image Restoration

items.summary: World action models (WAMs) predict actions and future observations, typically from a reconstruction-based representation that carries noisy, redundant information which can complicate downstream predictions. We introduce LeWAM, a bidirectional transformer for forward, backward, inverse dynamics and policy prediction, on a decoder-free JEPA latent trained end-to-end through all four modes. We see the following benefits: 1) Alignment: linear probes read robot and object state from LeWAM's latent better than from a regular Le World Model (a forward-only JEPA world model), while the latent ignores visual distractors as well as LeWM does and far better than a reconstruction-based WAM. 2) Acting: Closed-loop evaluations of LeWAM match a regular flow-matching policy trained on the same encoder at matched size, while also providing a world model. 3) Planning: Sampling raw actions when planning with WAMs lets MPC exploit dynamics-model inaccuracies; planning in the noise space of the policy head instead improves the closed-loop performance of these WAMs.
items.title: LeWAM: A JEPA World Action Model with Diffusion-Steering-Based MPC

items.summary: Semantic framework for preparing scientific simulation scenarios, validating typed configurations and qualifying numerical outputs with explicit provenance. One descriptor per software is compiled into an LLM contract, an ontology with SHACL shapes and FAIR metadata; three unchanged backends are linked at pinned revisions (TLS, LQL-Equiv, pyrcel). Outputs are synthetic and have not been validated against field measurements.
items.title: websemantic: a software-agnostic semantic layer from human intent to qualified simulated data

items.summary: While the volume of preserved research data and analysis software has grown significantly over the last decade, much of this valuable asset remains siloed in national or thematic repositories, in heterogeneous data and metadata formats that make dataset integration difficult. As a consequence, valuable scientific insights remain unexplored as researchers should spend increasing amounts of time with data discovery, interpretation, formatting and transformation. EOSC Data Commons (EDC) is building the next-generation federated research data infrastructure to eliminate cross-repository and cross-format data fragmentation. At the centre of the EDC technical architecture there are two complementary services, designed to bridge disconnected systems: EOSC Matchmaker: a discovery layer enabling researchers to discover datasets, software tools, and execution services across multiple scientific domains and EOSC Nodes. It operates alongside a catalogue of analytics tools that can be deployed close to the data, significantly reducing data movement and improving processing efficiency. EOSC Data Player: An execution platform integration service that provides harmonised APIs, shared metadata specifications, and common mechanisms for authentication, authorisation, and provenance tracking. This ensures that researchers can combine data and software tools from different providers without manually reconciling metadata formats or security protocols. To achieve scalable interoperability, the project uses a range of advanced semantic technologies, including knowledge graphs for rich metadata representation and standardised interfaces to support cross-infrastructure integration. EOSC Data Commons adopts community standards such as RO-Crate for packaging research artefacts and their metadata in a machine-actionable, highly interoperable manner. This technical stack is continuously validated through real-world use cases spanning diverse scientific domains. For data repositories, the technical frameworks established by EOSC Data Commons offer a highly practical blueprint. Testing EDC’s technological ecosystem through its open call, national repositories, such as ARP, can integrate with the broader European Open Science Cloud and expand their reach into new scientific communities, while maintaining their operational autonomy and data security. This presentation outlines the core technological solutions, semantic standards, and interoperability frameworks developed by EDC to enable seamless, cross-disciplinary data reuse. The talk aims to generate interest in the Hungarian ARP community to join the growing network of EDC repositories.
items.title: The Missing Link of EOSC: Interoperability of Data Repositories and Applications with EOSC Data Commons

items.summary: What if an AI agent could not complete a consequential action until the real-world result of an earlier, bounded action had been independently verified—and that verification was required to unlock the next execution step? As frontier AI models and autonomous agents increasingly operate financial systems, cloud infrastructure, sensitive communications, autonomous machinery, and critical infrastructure, conventional security mechanisms face a fundamental limitation: authorization establishes what is permitted, but does not necessarily establish what actually happened along the real execution path. Audit logs may record a mistake after its consequences become irreversible. Simulations may succeed while the real destination, network route, transaction system, or physical actuator behaves differently. Even a successful initial authorization does not justify unlimited authority to execute subsequent actions. This paper develops a different architectural principle: “Evidence is the key, not the log.” Building on the distinction that computation is not authority to act , the proposed architecture makes independently validated evidence of a preceding real effect a technical prerequisite for later effectuation. The mechanism is called Receipt-Gated Staged Effectuation , supported by an Interim Effectuation Validator (IEV) . For selected consequential operations, the architecture authorizes a deliberately bounded but real first effect, rather than immediately releasing the complete consequence. A protected observer, destination, transaction system, network element, storage component, or hardware controller generates an Effect Confirmation Receipt (ECR) describing what actually occurred. The IEV independently verifies the receipt against the authorized Candidate Act, expected effect, phase, destination, sink identity, freshness, policy, revocation state, and authorized scope. Only after successful validation does the protected domain establish the Continuation Authority Object (CAO) required for the next phase. The critical distinction is that the next effect can be made technically impossible—not merely prohibited by policy—until validated evidence from the preceding real effect becomes available. Possible implementations include receipt-derived cryptographic keys, split-key reconstruction, protected internal state, hardware latches, pre-staged non-executable commands, and pre-delivered ciphertext whose final decryption material remains withheld. Unlike ordinary canary deployment or post-execution monitoring, the earlier phase's evidence becomes part of the causal authority chain. Its receipt is not merely information about the previous operation; it is a required input to the authority enabling the next operation. The paper develops: Three effectuation modes: Direct protected single-phase execution, bounded demonstration followed by full effectuation, and progressive multi-phase execution. Adaptive effectuation: Geometric and risk-dependent progression, reversibility-aware phase sizing, nested stages, and parallel effectuation. Cryptographic causal dependency: Receipt-derived execution material, split credentials, tokenless continuation, hardware-gated enablement, and protected state transitions. Protected evidence semantics: Proof of delivery versus proof of effect, negative receipts, receipt freshness, destination binding, cross-device protection, Merkle receipt structures, and privacy-preserving confirmation. Independent continuation authority: Human, automatic, hybrid, and multi-authority decisions separated from the potentially compromised AI-agent environment. Fail-closed recovery: Missing or conflicting receipts, uncertain outcomes, replay protection, atomic consumption, reconciliation, and prevention of blind retries. Anti-bypass enforcement: Protected execution boundaries, credential surrogation, taint and provenance controls, alternative-path closure, and software–hardware implementation ind
items.title: Evidence Is the Key, Not the Log: Cryptographic Execution Control for AI Agents and Autonomous Systems

items.summary: We establish the overarching mathematical physics framework underlying gravitational screening and electroweak mixing in Big Boot Gauge Theory (BBGT). To demonstrate that the transition from the bare gravitational constant G_bare = 6.514085763e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 (derived from CODATA 2022 constants under unit space-time momentum p = mc = 1 kg m s^-1) to the observed value G_obs = 6.67430e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 is a rigorous topological necessity rather than an arbitrary post-hoc adjustment, we formulate the screening dynamics using Möbius inversion on finite posets over the subgroup lattice of Poincaré Dodecahedral Space (S^3/I^*). We prove that non-associative transit across the e_4 Pati-Salam midpoint node acts as a Möbius topological twist, fixing the geometric inverse-square screening factor S_ZIP^-2 = (1 - 1/120)^-2 = 1.016877348. Combining this with longitudinal Z-leakage (delta_Z = 0.026892000) and non-associative midpoint transit corrections (Delta_assoc = 0.000092701) yields the exact screened laboratory constant without arbitrary tuning.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that the weak mixing angle (sin^2 theta_W = 1/5 + 1/32 = 0.23125) originates from the pentagonal P_5 symmetry order of the dodecahedron combined with a 2^5 chiral energy cascade, agreeing with experiment (0.23122) to within 0.01%. Finally, we present the complete 8x8 Logical Transitive Index Matrix (T_{n->m}), showing how the 10^19 Planck-to-electroweak mass hierarchy is compressed down to a discrete compilation factor of 128.35 across the aethereal boot levels.

items.summary: This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.
items.title: Human Value Provenance - Measuring and Valuing Expert Human Knowledge Contributions in Generative AI Co-Creation

items.summary: This paper develops a new predefined-time integral reinforcement learning framework for optimal control of unknown nonlinear systems. The unknown drift is first approximated by a radial basis function (RBF) neural network, together with a data-driven online identification law for updating the corresponding neural weights. After the identifier converges to a sufficiently small neighborhood of the true dynamics, the learned model is incorporated into the integral reinforcement learning (IRL) problem. Unlike conventional reinforcement-learning-based optimal control, the desired convergence time is introduced directly into the control objective: a Lyapunov function and its prescribed decay behavior are specified by the designer, and inverse-optimal control is then used to construct a compatible running cost whose optimal policy inherits the predefined-time stabilization property. The value function is approximated by a second RBF neural network, and a new critic update law is developed to impose predefined-time convergence on the critic weights. Finite informative learning data are stored in a replay buffer and reused during the critic update, thereby avoiding the need for persistent excitation throughout the closed-loop operation. Theoretical analysis proves that the critic-weight error enters a prescribed residual set within the allocated learning horizon, while the closed-loop state reaches a small neighborhood of the origin within the overall designer-specified deadline. Numerical simulations on an unknown nonlinear system verify accurate drift reconstruction, predefined-time critic learning, and closed-loop convergence.
items.title: Predefined-Time Integral Reinforcement Learning for Unknown Nonlinear Systems via Inverse-Optimal Design

What consumes that budget, and why does it fail to produce results? We diagnose these costs and failures through a multi-axis open-coding study of 200 CyberGym traces, spanning four agents (i.e., Codex, OpenCode, Cybench, and EnIGMA) under an unaided baseline and four existing efficiency methods. The study reveals three key findings. First, different agents vary substantially in success and cost, and higher spending does not consistently yield better outcomes. Second, code localization and understanding, together with vulnerability reasoning and trigger design, account for 60.4% of tokens and represent the two leading bottlenecks in failed runs. Third, only 24.4% of matched comparisons preserve success at lower total cost; unsuitable signals and auxiliary overhead limit the benefits of existing methods. Motivated by these findings, we present AVRI, an Agent-centric Vulnerability Reasoning Interface built around a persistent Bidirectional Evidence Trace (BET). BET connects how the harness consumes input with the conditions required to make a selected operation unsafe, retaining source-supported correspondences alongside the agent's hypotheses and open questions. Reading, analysis, and persistence commands help agents build and reuse this evidence rather than repeatedly retrieve and reconstruct it. On 20 evaluation tasks, AVRI reduces total cost by 18.0% for Codex and 23.7% for OpenCode while preserving success rates and improving or maintaining recall.
items.title: Where Do the Tokens Go? Understanding and Reducing Costs in LLM Agents for Vulnerability Discovery

items.summary: Physics-informed machine learning has gained significant attention in recent years. In regimes of limited data, parametrized Gaussian processes have become popular. Existing approaches, however, often face limitations, such as requiring parametrizable (also called controllable) systems or a large number of output tasks. In this work, we introduce a systematic procedure we call "ghost tasking", using auxiliary tasks to circumvent these limitations. We prove that such ghost tasks can render any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling algorithmic construction of parametrized Gaussian Processes while keeping the number of required tasks (i.e. output dimensions) and latent functions low. We find that ghost tasking performs especially well in an inverse problem setting, even with very few available data. We show the usage and power of ghost tasking in three experiments, providing systematic comparisons to the only other currently available method applicable to all experiments. We provide necessary syntax and explications for two computer algebra programs that compute parametrizations for systems with polynomial or rational coefficients. Our theoretical results extend to systems with meromorphic functions.
items.title: Ghost tasking for parametrized Gaussian Processes solving linear differential equations

items.summary: What if an AI agent could not complete a consequential action until the real-world result of an earlier, bounded action had been independently verified—and that verification was required to unlock the next execution step? As frontier AI models and autonomous agents increasingly operate financial systems, cloud infrastructure, sensitive communications, autonomous machinery, and critical infrastructure, conventional security mechanisms face a fundamental limitation: authorization establishes what is permitted, but does not necessarily establish what actually happened along the real execution path. Audit logs may record a mistake after its consequences become irreversible. Simulations may succeed while the real destination, network route, transaction system, or physical actuator behaves differently. Even a successful initial authorization does not justify unlimited authority to execute subsequent actions. This paper develops a different architectural principle: “Evidence is the key, not the log.” Building on the distinction that computation is not authority to act , the proposed architecture makes independently validated evidence of a preceding real effect a technical prerequisite for later effectuation. The mechanism is called Receipt-Gated Staged Effectuation , supported by an Interim Effectuation Validator (IEV) . For selected consequential operations, the architecture authorizes a deliberately bounded but real first effect, rather than immediately releasing the complete consequence. A protected observer, destination, transaction system, network element, storage component, or hardware controller generates an Effect Confirmation Receipt (ECR) describing what actually occurred. The IEV independently verifies the receipt against the authorized Candidate Act, expected effect, phase, destination, sink identity, freshness, policy, revocation state, and authorized scope. Only after successful validation does the protected domain establish the Continuation Authority Object (CAO) required for the next phase. The critical distinction is that the next effect can be made technically impossible—not merely prohibited by policy—until validated evidence from the preceding real effect becomes available. Possible implementations include receipt-derived cryptographic keys, split-key reconstruction, protected internal state, hardware latches, pre-staged non-executable commands, and pre-delivered ciphertext whose final decryption material remains withheld. Unlike ordinary canary deployment or post-execution monitoring, the earlier phase's evidence becomes part of the causal authority chain. Its receipt is not merely information about the previous operation; it is a required input to the authority enabling the next operation. The paper develops: Three effectuation modes: Direct protected single-phase execution, bounded demonstration followed by full effectuation, and progressive multi-phase execution. Adaptive effectuation: Geometric and risk-dependent progression, reversibility-aware phase sizing, nested stages, and parallel effectuation. Cryptographic causal dependency: Receipt-derived execution material, split credentials, tokenless continuation, hardware-gated enablement, and protected state transitions. Protected evidence semantics: Proof of delivery versus proof of effect, negative receipts, receipt freshness, destination binding, cross-device protection, Merkle receipt structures, and privacy-preserving confirmation. Independent continuation authority: Human, automatic, hybrid, and multi-authority decisions separated from the potentially compromised AI-agent environment. Fail-closed recovery: Missing or conflicting receipts, uncertain outcomes, replay protection, atomic consumption, reconciliation, and prevention of blind retries. Anti-bypass enforcement: Protected execution boundaries, credential surrogation, taint and provenance controls, alternative-path closure, and software–hardware implementation ind
items.title: Evidence Is the Key, Not the Log: Cryptographic Execution Control for AI Agents and Autonomous Systems

items.summary: Supporting research data for physical-state supervision of design-only Gaussian process surrogates, with optional mixture-of-experts comparisons. Includes 1,987 CH designs, 3,000 thermal-explosion designs, 3,000 recalculated Be/Cocktail designs, state diagnostics, saved predictions, paired evaluation metrics, learning curves, grid diagnostics, timing records and file-level provenance. The data record does not include software, solver binaries, material libraries or raw trajectories. Grid sensitivities and historical reproduction limitations are documented in README.md. Data and accompanying documentation are licensed under CC BY 4.0.
items.title: Physical-state supervision for design-only Gaussian process surrogates of implosion simulations: supporting data

items.summary: Long-horizon robotic manipulation is often built by chaining independently trained skills. Although each skill can be reliable in isolation, performance degrades sharply when skills are chained: each downstream skill must start from the state its predecessor leaves behind rather than from its training distribution. We study this failure mode, Observation-Space Shift (OSS), and ask what causes these skill-seam failures. Using privileged simulator resets, we find that the dominant shift comes from displaced scene state (e.g., an open drawer or secondary objects left behind by earlier skills), not from the robot's joint configuration or the object the downstream skill manipulates. To test this diagnosis, we build a fully learned detect-restore-resume system: a task-progress monitor detects the stall, a learned policy restores the displaced scene components, and seam-robust fine-tuning lets the skill resume. It recovers the seam where every tested alternative fails, which we treat as evidence for the diagnosis rather than as a general-purpose method. On the BOSS-44 benchmark, the system improves full-chain success from 7.6% to 26.5%, a 3.5x improvement over the base policy and 51% of a privileged restoration oracle, whereas best-of-K resampling, a Diffusion Policy, and world-model baselines fail to recover from the evaluated seam states. On a real Franka arm running a fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ policy, the same monitor is limited by exterior-camera observability, yet closing the loop still recovers some otherwise-terminal failures, motivating wrist and gripper sensing. These results suggest that some long-horizon composition failures are better addressed by restoring the scene before resuming the policy than by retrying from an off-support state.
items.title: Diagnosing and Recovering from Observation-Space Shift at Long-Horizon Skill Seams

items.summary: Some defects in an AI-generated study can be identified from its artifacts; others require knowledge of what was approved before execution. We propose study contracts that bind declared experimental choices, run obligations and claim scope to recorded execution evidence, and distinguish this contract-relative verification from scientific truth. A diagnostic using eight self-authored clean/mutated pairs illustrates the information boundary. A deterministic checker applying a registered, fault-specific rule to approved and executed objects detected all eight registered mutations. Across eighteen recorded judge aliases given individual metadata-filtered packages without pair context or the registry-selected fault label, 104 of 144 mutated evaluation cases received defect flags; the remaining cases comprised 32 abstentions and eight terminal failures, with no explicit clean decisions on mutated cases. Some packages retained approval and execution fields, including digests. The prompt instructed judges to abstain when evidence was insufficient. These results characterize a deliberately information-asymmetric development setting; they do not isolate the effect of authoritative information from differences in task specification and rule selection, and they are not comparative verifier quality or agent reward hacking. We identify full-information comparisons, legitimate-adaptation controls and closed-loop agent evaluations as necessary tests of whether contract checks improve useful compliant completion under optimization.
items.title: What Output-Only Review Cannot Verify: Study Contracts for Research Agents

items.summary: A customer attempts an online booking, receives no confirmation, and finds that the support form requires a booking number that was never issued. No one has rejected the claim; the procedure cannot even receive it. This paper argues that such failures are not merely problems of customer service. They raise a question of justice. When a business controls the ordinary route through which consumers assert contractual rights, it bears responsibility for the avoidable and disproportionate burdens created by that route. The paper calls this principle procedural responsibility . Survey data show that the anticipated effort of complaining is a common reason for doing nothing. Among consumers who experienced a problem but took no action, 57 percent expected complaining to take too long and 43 percent expected it to be too complicated (Consumer Conditions Scoreboard 2025). European and German law address parts of this problem, and Spain's 2025 customer-support law demonstrates that legislators can establish specific procedural duties. Yet a coherent cross-sector standard for accessible, traceable and substantive complaint handling remains missing in EU and German law. The paper proposes five rights: reciprocal communication, a continuing case record, human reconsideration of unresolved claims, timely handling of urgent matters, and access to relevant evidence. It also outlines proportionate remedies for objectively established procedural failures that do not require another exhausting complaint. The goal is not to guarantee that consumers win disputes, but to ensure that their claims can be received, examined and meaningfully decided. The principle applies from letters and call centres to chatbots and AI agents, offering a concrete direction for the European Commission's planned Digital Fairness Act.
items.title: The Cost of Having Rights: Why a Consumer Complaint Is a Question of Justice, Not Customer Service

items.summary: This paper presents a diagnostic theory that interprets a phenomenon observed in advanced economies—monetary easing and standard macroeconomic policies no longer generating sustained growth, even as they are accompanied by improvements in employment—not as a "failure of policy management" or a temporary demand shortfall, but as the structural depletion of investment outlets. As its core concepts, this paper introduces the structural frontier coefficient Φ, which represents the latent constraint determined by demographics, the institutional environment, and capital structure, and the critical threshold θ, at which policy effects undergo a qualitative shift. It further presents the "demand-constrained growth hypothesis" as the mechanism through which the structural frontier becomes constraining as the economy matures. The paper divides demand-side constraints into four types of goods—time-constrained goods, goods with strong ownership constraints, goods with weak ownership constraints and multiple ownership, and conduit goods—and organizes demand displacement and qualitative-improvement constraints as cross-cutting constraints superimposed on them. In an economy whose room for quantitative expansion has shrunk, the center of growth shifts to qualitative improvement; however, as the quality frontier is approached, the marginal cost of improvement rises while marginal utility and the scope for price pass-through may decline, so that technological progress may diverge from growth in sales and GDP. In the region Φ > θ, Solow-type growth theory and New Keynesian transmission may, by and large, function effectively, whereas in the region Φ ≤ θ, the spillover of monetary easing to real investment and sustained growth weakens, and easing tends instead to spill over into alternative channels such as asset prices, fund retention, and external capital movements. On the other hand, because the sensitivity of the employment channel to Φ is relatively lower than that of the growth channel, employment responses may remain relatively intact even in the region Φ ≤ θ. This asymmetry of the dual channels explains the simultaneous occurrence of employment improvement and growth stagnation. Under the definitional constraint that Φ is not back-calculated from outcome variables, this paper presents a two-layer diagnostic identification procedure. The structural state is diagnosed from the component-wise directions (structural signature) of the ordinal scale Φ̂, which is constructed without using outcome variables, and from the binding constraint; the policy transmission state is classified separately by the responses of the growth and alternative channels to identified monetary policy shocks (employment responses are checked as an auxiliary diagnosis); the two are then compared, with the estimate a of the realized investment ratio α, the cost-push coefficient κ, and other measures reported alongside as auxiliary findings. Furthermore, under the hypothesis that in mature, constrained regimes the elasticity of substitution declines and the dominant bottleneck determines the viability of investment, the paper positions the min approximation not as a predictive function but as a diagnostic limit. Companion empirical paper. This record also contains the companion empirical paper, "Does a Structural-Constraint Diagnosis Predict the Effectiveness of Monetary Easing? Exploratory Evidence from Within-Country Comparisons with Judgments Fixed before Matching" (Version 3, September 2026; English and Japanese PDFs, files named Watanabe_2026_*_Empirical_v3.pdf), which tests the central proposition of this paper.
items.title: General Theory of Structural Constraints: Investment Trap, Demand-Constrained Growth, and Regime Shifts in Monetary Policy Transmission

items.summary: Rationale. Implantation of permanent pacemakers in patients after repeat cardiac surgery can be significantly limited by cicatricial changes, recent cannulations, and obliteration of conventional venous accesses. An additional complication is the presence of congenital variants of systemic venous return, primarily persistent left superior vena cava (PSVC), which alters the geometry of endocardial electrode placement and increases the risk of technical complications. Case Description: This patient presented with a complex cardiac surgical history: aortic coarctation reconstruction in 2013, David I surgery in December 2025, and subsequent emergency hospitalization for decompensated chronic heart failure secondary to aortic valve avulsion and severe aortic regurgitation. On June 10, 2026, the patient underwent repeat aortic valve replacement with a Perceval L seamless biological valve prosthesis for life-saving reasons. In the early postoperative period, manifestations of sick sinus syndrome persisted, with transient second-degree sinoatrial block and pauses up to 3950 ms. Therefore, implantation of a dual-chamber, rate-adaptive pacemaker was planned for June 12, 2026. Intraoperatively, the standard right-sided approach was deemed unacceptable due to a fresh postoperative wound, severe tissue edema, and recent cannulation of the right subclavian artery. Upon conversion to the left subclavian approach, a stented septal vein (SVC) was detected with drainage through the dilated coronary sinus into the right atrium. Given preserved atrioventricular conduction, severe hypocoagulation, thrombocytopenia, and a high risk of coronary sinus injury, a decision was made to abandon the ventricular lead and perform single-chamber atrial pacing in AAIR mode. The lead with active fixation was successfully advanced through the splanchnic vein and the coronary sinus into the right atrium. Conclusion. This clinical observation demonstrates that in a patient with sick sinus syndrome and preserved atrioventricular conduction, AAIR mode can be a reasonable and technically safe option for permanent pacing when standard venous access is impossible and there is a high risk of ventricular lead placement through an anomalous venous collector.
items.title: FORCED INTRAOPERATIVE MODIFICATION OF PERMANENT CARDIAC PACING TACTICS THROUGH PERSISTENT LEFT SUPERIOR VENA CAVATA IN A HIGH-RISK PATIENT FOR CARDIAC SURGERY: A CASE REPORT

items.summary: Self-contained computational materials accompanying "Verifiable approval-release decisions for construction project management: A provenance-aware contract and automated evidence" by Ahmad Baghdadi. Version 4.0.0 includes source code, complete generated inputs and results, schemas, exact witnesses, a de-identified calendar encoding, benchmark records and SHA-256 checksums. This version adds 83 conventional priority-list levelling comparisons under identical constraints: 72 tied peaks and 11 one-gate improvements, with sufficient exact certificates for all 83. A complete two-plan PROV-O example passes the domain and provenance SHACL profiles and preserves every decision field after RDF exchange. The suite comprises 145 automated tests. Earlier computational evidence includes generated extraction, 360 controlled record comparisons, exact wave bounds, nine calendar scenarios and 80 saved benchmark plans with renewed arithmetic audit. S14 preparation includes blank independent-annotation and approval registers plus a precision/recall evaluator with explicit denominators. No native baseline or independent annotations are available; field validation has not been executed. Case A remains historical aggregates only. Calendar B is a prior encoding with assumed review windows. Supplementary Table S1 identifies the deposited components and the supplement consolidates the evidence limits.
items.title: Reproducibility materials for verifiable approval-release decisions in construction project management

items.summary: Recent achievements in AI-assisted mathematics require intensive interaction of agents with proof assistants to generate machine-checked proof certificates. Agents interact with proof assistants such as Rocq or Lean through an interface that controls what the agent receives from the prover and the cost of these interactions. Today, these interfaces are adapted from tools designed for humans and not optimized for agents. We propose an evolutionary method where a frontier model incrementally proposes new features and only keeps the ones that improve the overall performance of smaller models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by growing, on a curated set of mathematical problems, ROCQ-MCP-EVOLVE, a new MCP server for the Rocq prover. On the held-out test split of miniF2F-Rocq, an agent equipped with ROCQ-MCP-EVOLVE outperforms both the baseline that only exposes the Rocq compiler and an established MCP server, across four models from two families, in success rate, cost per solve, and time per solve. Although evolved for Rocq, the resulting server transfers to Lean, improving cost and time per solve on a subset of PutnamBench. We release ROCQ-MCP-EVOLVE and its port to Lean.
items.title: Growing an Agent/Prover Interface: Evolutionary Tool Design for Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving in Rocq and Lean

items.summary: Analysis code and computed evidence store for the manuscript "An exact recurrence test for acquisition-chain bounds in vehicle telemetry: the closed ECU surface yields nothing, and the one detection lies in the logger we built ourselves", submitted to Sensors and Actuators A: Physical. This deposit contains code and derived results only. The underlying telemetry is published separately under its own DOIs, which fetch_data.py downloads and checksum-verifies before analysis, so the published figures are reproducible from the public record. Study design: observational audit of already-deposited telemetry (seven recording sessions). No experimental control, no intervention, no independent replication, and no statistical power for population-level inference. Headlines formulated after measurement rather than pre-declared in config.json are labelled exploratory in the manuscript. Multiplicity: this deposit is one of 15 analyses drawn from the same corpus of seven sessions, one vehicle and one rider. No correction for multiple comparisons is applied across that family, so the family-wise error rate is not controlled. Repository commit of record: 37f7b2147b26
items.title: Reproducibility package (I-21): An exact recurrence test for acquisition-chain bounds in vehicle telemetry: the closed ECU surface yields nothing, and the one detection lies in the logger we built ourselves

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a comment on a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview and comments at https://prereview.org/reviews/22745390 . Thank you, Evgenii, for the detailed and constructive PREreview. Your comments led us to substantially strengthen both the experimental design and the interpretation of the results. We have now released a revised version of the manuscript that addresses the main points raised in the review. The revision includes: A 30-seed robustness analysis rather than relying on a single simulation seed A correlation sweep for estimator errors from ρ = 0 to 0.8 Regression-fitted and test-set oracle aggregation baselines Shared-noise experiments for the model–collective calibration signal, reported with ROC-AUC and lift Explicit specification of the four-Wave rolling calibration window, software versions, and PCG64 RNG Portfolio scaling to 100 Feature Blocks using an exact binary MILP reference An explicit separation between budget-constrained portfolio selection and ODP's native dependency-aware sequencing role An exact and scaling benchmark for ODP sequencing under prerequisite constraints An explicit competing-interest disclosure A public reproducibility package containing the simulation code, deterministic seeds, generated data, analysis scripts, and validation material. One particularly useful outcome of the revision was that the stronger experiments narrowed some of our original claims. For example, inverse-MSE aggregation performs very strongly when estimator errors are independent, but its advantage collapses under strong shared error. We also found that ODP distance is not the strongest heuristic for budget-constrained portfolio selection, while it performs very differently in its native sequencing role, where ERS/BVS is exactly optimal for the declared objective without dependencies and remains close to the exact optimum under the tested prerequisite constraints. Revised manuscript: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10648 Reproducibility package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23261325 Thank you again for the review. It improved the paper. Competing interests I am a co-author of the manuscript discussed in this PREreview and a contributor to the D-POAF framework evaluated in the study. I am also affiliated with Inovionix, which develops software implementing D-POAF concepts.
items.title: Comment on a PREreview of "Governed Human-AI Prioritization Under Uncertainty: Adaptive Estimation and Dependency-Constrained Portfolio Selection"

items.summary: It is assumed that a natural way to improve the pedagogical quality of large language model tutors is to define a metric of instructional performance and fine-tune the model against it. To test this strategy, we designed a metric of pedagogical adaptivity that scores each instructional decision in a learning sequence against the conditions of the learning situation, which is the standard used for automated pedagogical scoring. We audited a frontier tutor across 2,000 learner scenarios, corrected its weakest cases by fine-tuning an open-weights proxy, and asked 31 trained educators to rate the pedagogical alignment of the outputs blind, before and after correction. The metric increased from +0.05 to +0.42 for the corrected cases, while the expert ratings decreased from 4.46 to 3.03, with the unmodified controls remaining unchanged and a base-proxy control ruling out the change of model. The tutor performed worse because any metric that scores decisions independently and averages them is maximized by repeating the single best decision, and the fine-tuned model collapsed to that exact optimum in every case, in and out of sample. Educators identified the repetition, which such metrics cannot represent, and preserving the learner's trajectory in the score reduced, but did not reverse, the metric's verdict. Weight analysis traced the correction to the model's output projection, where it had memorized its training strings rather than learned to adapt. We conclude that measurement validity does not imply optimization validity, and we derive design principles for benchmarks that assess or train AI-tutor instruction.
items.title: The learner who does not learn: when optimizing a pedagogical metric degrades LLM tutoring

items.summary: This repository contains the replication data and R code accompanying the study “From Periodic VAT Listings to Real-Time Reporting: Digital Reporting Requirements, Business Information Architecture and the EU VAT Compliance Gap”. The replication package combines European Commission VAT compliance gap data with a manually verified longitudinal coding of mandatory Digital Reporting Requirements across 26 European Union Member States over 2013–2023. The analytical panel contains 284 country-year observations. The policy coding harmonises periodic VAT listings and control statements, SAF-T and invoice-data reporting systems, and continuous or near-real-time transaction controls within a common information-governance framework. Alternative coding scenarios are retained to document uncertainty associated with implementation dates, phased rollouts and differences in reporting architecture. The accompanying R scripts reproduce the analytical dataset construction, descriptive statistics, two-way fixed-effects models, country-specific trend specifications, first-difference analysis, alternative treatment codings, architecture comparisons, panel diagnostics, staggered-adoption diagnostics and wild-cluster bootstrap inference reported in the study. No pre-computed analytical results are included in the repository. All derived results can be reproduced from the supplied input workbook and R scripts. The underlying VAT compliance gap data originate from the European Commission, Directorate-General for Taxation and Customs Union. The original DRR coding and its documentation were compiled by the authors from official European Commission and national tax-administration sources. The authors’ original data compilation and policy coding are made available under CC BY 4.0. The R replication code is released under the MIT License. Underlying third-party data remain subject to the terms of their original providers.
items.title: Replication Data and R Code for "From Periodic VAT Listings to Real-Time Reporting: Digital Reporting Requirements and the EU VAT Compliance Gap"

items.summary: DSM–861 is best understood as a deterministic spectral computing architecture built from a rigid finite graph, a toroidal Hodge geometry, nonlinear KAN transport, vorton-inspired skew coupling, and associative-memory snapping. The arithmetic anchor is 861 = 42,2= T41 = 3 · 7 · 41,  while the interaction topology is exactly J(42, 2) with degree 80 and spectrum {80, 38, −2}. The toroidal layer supplies a genuine discrete differential calculus. The finite-state theorem fixes the exact nine-qubit boundary of a single 861-dimensional core. The controllability theorem converts universal computation into a concrete Lie-algebra calculation. The snapping theorem supplies a mathematically correct route to non-accumulating numerical error through a deliberately constructed quadratic attractor. The resulting program is therefore executable as mathematics and engineering. Build the graph. Build the Hodge operators. Construct the control generators. Compute their Lie closure. Implement the nonlinear snap. Measure the ϵ2 law. Synthesize the FPGA. Then benchmark complete circuits. If those tests succeed, DSM–861 becomes a demonstrated deterministic spectral processor rather than merely a conceptual analogy to quantum computing.
items.title: Deterministic Spectral Quantum Emulation on Classical Hardware

items.summary: We detail scalable methods for approximating the quadratic entropy $p^T d p$ for arbitrary distributions $p$ and common distances $d$ of negative type. We focus on the Euclidean and spherical geodesic cases, which both use random feature embeddings and projections to dramatically improve computational complexity within a simple framework. Amortization of a single large matrix multiplication and control variates further enable computation at large scale with low memory and runtime in situations where $d$ is held constant while $p$ varies. We demonstrate this with a comparison against direct pair sampling and bibliometric/scientometric examples on Open Graph Benchmark datasets, revealing papers, fields, and institutions with both particularly narrow and broad interdisciplinary reach from their citations and text features alone.
items.title: Efficient quadratic entropy with distance sketches

items.summary: The present study was undertaken to establish pharmacognostic standards and phytochemical profiles of two ethnomedicinally important plants, Cajanus goensis and Sarcostigma kleinii. Both species are traditionally employed in the treatment of rheumatism, inflammatory disorders, and other systemic ailments, yet scientific validation of their crude drug parameters remains limited. Standardization of herbal materials is essential to ensure identity, purity, and reproducibility, thereby reducing variability and enhancing therapeutic reliability. In this study, plant materials were procured from authentic local sources—Cajanus goensis from Udaipur, Rajasthan, and Sarcostigma kleinii from Latur, Maharashtra—and subjected to comprehensive pharmacognostic and phytochemical evaluation. Organoleptic analysis revealed distinct sensory characteristics, with Cajanus goensis exhibiting greenish-brown coloration, earthy odor, and coarse texture, while Sarcostigma kleinii showed yellowish-brown coloration, pungent odor, and oily texture. Macroscopic and microscopic examinations confirmed diagnostic features such as dorsiventral leaves, reticulate venation, thick cuticular layers, and prominent vascular bundles. Physico-chemical evaluation demonstrated that ash values, extractive values, moisture content, and pH were within pharmacopoeial limits, thereby confirming the purity and stability of the crude drugs. Notably, Cajanus goensis exhibited higher alcohol-soluble extractives, while Sarcostigma kleinii showed greater water-soluble extractives, reflecting differences in phytoconstituent solubility. Phytochemical screening revealed the presence of carbohydrates, amino acids, alkaloids, glycosides, flavonoids, tannins, and phenolic compounds in both species. Proteins were detected only in Sarcostigma kleinii, while saponins were present exclusively in Cajanus goensis. Sterols were absent in both plants, highlighting unique chemical signatures that aid in authentication. Quantitative estimation confirmed that both species are rich in flavonoids and phenolic compounds, with Sarcostigma kleinii showing slightly higher concentrations (21.06 ± 1.000 mg/g quercetin equivalents and 21.19 ± 0.854 mg/g tannic acid equivalents) compared to Cajanus goensis (19.09 ± 0.444 mg/g and 18.49 ± 0.033 mg/g, respectively). These bioactive constituents are well recognized for their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, supporting the traditional use of these plants in rheumatism and related disorders. In conclusion, the study provides reproducible pharmacognostic and phytochemical data for Cajanus goensis and Sarcostigma kleinii, thereby validating their ethnomedicinal claims and establishing a foundation for further pharmacological investigations. The results underscore the importance of standardization in herbal medicine and highlight the potential of these crude drugs as reliable sources of bioactive compounds for future therapeutic applications.
tags: Cajanus goensis; Sarcostigma kleinii; crude drug standardization; phytochemical screening; flavonoids; phenolic compounds; rheumatism; pharmacognosy; herbal medicine; quality control.
items.title: Standardization And Phytochemical Profiling of Cajanus Goensis and Sarcostigma Kleinii: Establishing Baseline Parameters for Crude Drug Evaluation

items.summary: Physics-informed machine learning has gained significant attention in recent years. In regimes of limited data, parametrized Gaussian processes have become popular. Existing approaches, however, often face limitations, such as requiring parametrizable (also called controllable) systems or a large number of output tasks. In this work, we introduce a systematic procedure we call "ghost tasking", using auxiliary tasks to circumvent these limitations. We prove that such ghost tasks can render any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling algorithmic construction of parametrized Gaussian Processes while keeping the number of required tasks (i.e. output dimensions) and latent functions low. We find that ghost tasking performs especially well in an inverse problem setting, even with very few available data. We show the usage and power of ghost tasking in three experiments, providing systematic comparisons to the only other currently available method applicable to all experiments. We provide necessary syntax and explications for two computer algebra programs that compute parametrizations for systems with polynomial or rational coefficients. Our theoretical results extend to systems with meromorphic functions.
items.title: Ghost tasking for parametrized Gaussian Processes solving linear differential equations
